title: Common fixed vector for a group of unipotent matrices
statement: Let $K$ be any field [def-weil-field] and let $d\geq1$ be an integer. Let $H\subseteq\operatorname{GL}_d(K)$ be a subgroup of the group of invertible $d\times d$ matrices over $K$ (so $H$ contains $I_d$ and is closed under matrix multiplication and inversion). Suppose that for each $h\in H$ there exists an integer $N_h\geq1$ such that $(h-I_d)^{N_h}=0$. Then there exists a column vector $v\in K^d$ such that $v\ne0$ and $hv=v$ for every $h\in H$. No finiteness, commutativity, algebraicity or connectedness assumption is made on $H$.

source.place: Proposition 14.1, printed pp.279--280 (an abstract group acting unipotently on a nonzero finite-dimensional vector space has a nonzero common fixed vector), specialized to a subgroup of GL_d(K).

proof.text: Choose an algebraic closure $L$ of $K$ using [lem-pc-algebraic-closure-exists-unique], and identify $K$ with its image in $L$. View each $h\in H$ as a matrix over $L$. Its inverse over $K$ remains its inverse over $L$, and its given equation $(h-I_d)^{N_h}=0$ remains true entry by entry. Thus the same abstract group $H$ acts on the nonzero space $L^d$ by unipotent operators. We will descend a fixed vector at the end; there is no assumption that $H$ is finite.

source.place: Proposition 14.1, printed p.279: replacement of the base field by its algebraic closure; footnote 1.

proof.text: Among the nonzero $H$-stable $L$-subspaces of $L^d$ choose $W$ of smallest dimension: these dimensions form a nonempty set of positive integers, since $L^d$ itself is allowed. A nonzero proper stable subspace of $W$ would have smaller dimension (extend its basis to one of $W$), so none exists. Put $r_h=h|_W$. Since $h^{-1}$ also preserves $W$, these are invertible and $r_{gh}=r_g r_h$. Restricting the polynomial equation to $W$ gives $(r_h-I_W)^{N_h}=0$.

source.place: Proposition 14.1, printed p.279: replacement of the representation by a simple submodule.

proof.text: Put $A=\operatorname{span}_L\{r_h:h\in H\}\subseteq\operatorname{End}_L(W)$. This span is a unital subalgebra: $r_1=I_W$ and $r_g r_h=r_{gh}$ show closure under products of finite sums. An $A$-stable subspace is $H$-stable and conversely; hence $W$ is a faithful simple left $A$-module. By [lem-sfb-simple-algebra-scalar-endomorphisms], $C=\operatorname{End}_A(W)$ consists exactly of the scalar maps from $L$. An $L$-basis of $W$ therefore generates $W$ as a $C$-module. Apply [lem-sfb-finite-simple-double-centralizer] to $(A,W)$: any $L$-linear endomorphism $f$ is additive and commutes with every scalar map, so is $C$-linear, and the cited surjectivity gives $a\in A$ acting as $f$. Since $A$ acts by its inclusion in $\operatorname{End}_L(W)$, this says $A=\operatorname{End}_L(W)$.

source.place: Proposition 14.1, printed pp.279–280: double-centralizer theorem and scalar endomorphisms, giving A=End_k(V).

proof.text: Let $J=\operatorname{span}_L\{r_h-I_W:h\in H\}\subseteq A$. It is a two-sided ideal: for $g,h\in H$, $$r_g(r_h-I_W)=(r_{gh}-I_W)-(r_g-I_W),\qquad (r_h-I_W)r_g=(r_{hg}-I_W)-(r_g-I_W),$$ and bilinearity extends these inclusions to all of $A$ and $J$. By [lem-pc-finite-dimensional-nilpotent-trace], each $r_h-I_W$ has trace zero, since its power $N_h$ is zero and $W$ is finite-dimensional. Trace is the sum of diagonal entries by [def-weil-endomorphism-trace], so finite linear combinations also have trace zero. Choose a basis of $W$; since $\dim_L W\geq1$, the matrix unit $E_{11}\in A$ has trace $1\ne0$. Hence $J\ne A$.

source.place: Proposition 14.1, printed p.280: the span J is an ideal and every element of J has trace zero.

proof.text: We show directly that a proper two-sided ideal $J$ of $A=\operatorname{End}_L(W)$ must be zero. Otherwise choose $x\in J$ with a nonzero matrix entry $x_{ij}$. For every pair of basis indices $a,b$, matrix multiplication gives $E_{ai}xE_{jb}=x_{ij}E_{ab}\in J$. Scaling by $x_{ij}^{-1}$ puts every $E_{ab}$ in $J$; these matrices span $A$, contradicting $J\ne A$. Consequently $J=0$. Since $r_h-I_W\in J$, all $r_h$ are $I_W$. Any nonzero $w\in W\subseteq L^d$ is therefore fixed by every $h\in H$.

source.place: Proposition 14.1, printed p.280: simplicity of the full matrix algebra; the matrix-unit calculation supplies the elementary argument.

proof.text: It remains to descend the fixed vector $w=(w_1,\ldots,w_d)\ne0$. Choose a $K$-basis $c_1,\ldots,c_t$ of the $K$-span in $L$ of its finitely many coordinates, and write $w=\sum_{j=1}^t c_j v_j$ with $v_j\in K^d$. For every $h\in H$, $0=(h-I_d)w=\sum_j c_j(h-I_d)v_j$. The entries of $(h-I_d)v_j$ lie in $K$, so independence of the $c_j$ gives $(h-I_d)v_j=0$ for every $j$. Some $v_j$ is nonzero, because $w\ne0$. Fixing such a $j$ gives a single nonzero vector in $K^d$ fixed by all of $H$. This coefficient comparison works simultaneously for arbitrarily many $h$.

source.place: Proposition 14.1, printed p.279, footnote 1: fixed vectors descend under scalar extension; explicit finite coordinate-span argument.

proof_origin.place: Proposition 14.1, printed pp.279–280, including footnote 1; minimal-dimension, matrix-unit and coefficient-comparison details written out.
